title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms

Download Course Handout (PDF)







NoteAbout the Course





This course is an advanced study that follows Data Structures and Algorithms. It is designed to equip students with a deep understanding of major algorithmic design paradigms and the techniques required for their rigorous analysis. The curriculum covers the formal analysis of algorithm correctness, time complexity, and space complexity, as well as computational complexity theory including NP‑completeness.









NoteTarget Audience





Summer Term course meant for people who want to improve their course grade.









NotePrerequisites





Data Structures and Algorithms (CS F213) or equivalent. Working knowledge of programming in C/C++ or Python.

title: Randomized Algorithms
text:
← Practice






NoteProblem E1



Distinguish Las Vegas and Monte Carlo randomized algorithms. Give one example of each type from the course.








TipSolution





Las Vegas: always correct, randomized runtime (e.g., randomized quicksort). Monte Carlo: bounded error, deterministic runtime (e.g., Freivalds’ algorithm).









NoteProblem E2



Freivalds’ algorithm for checking AB = C picks r \in \{0,1\}^n uniformly and checks A(Br) = Cr. If AB \neq C, what is the maximum probability that the test passes (false positive)? Assume all arithmetic is mod a prime p > 2.








TipSolution





If AB \neq C, then D = AB - C \neq 0 is a non-zero matrix. The test passes if Dr = 0 for random r \in \{0,1\}^n. Since D \neq 0, there is at least one non-zero row. For a non-zero row vector d \neq 0, \Pr[d \cdot r = 0] \le 1/2. So overall \Pr[Dr=0] \le 1/2.









NoteProblem E3



You run Freivalds’ algorithm once and it says AB = C. What can you conclude? If it says AB \neq C, what can you conclude? Now suppose you run the test k times independently and it passes every time. What is the probability of error after k runs? How many runs are needed to achieve error < \epsilon?








TipSolution





If the test passes, AB = C with probability at least 1/2 (one-sided error: false positives possible). If it fails, AB \neq C with certainty (no false negatives). After k independent passes, error \le (1/2)^k. For error < \epsilon, need k > \log_2(1/\epsilon).









NoteProblem E4



Consider the following Monte Carlo algorithm: to check if an array A[1..n] has a majority element, pick a random index i and check whether A[i] appears more than n/2 times in A.

If a majority element exists, what is the probability that one random pick finds it?
How many independent picks are needed to find a majority element with probability at least 1 - \delta?
Is this a Las Vegas or Monte Carlo algorithm? Justify.









TipSolution






If a majority element exists, it occupies > n/2 positions. Probability a random pick hits it: > (n/2)/n = 1/2.
With k independent picks, failure probability (never picking the majority) < (1/2)^k. To get failure < \delta, need k > \log_2(1/\delta).
Monte Carlo — the algorithm has one-sided error: if it returns an element, that element is guaranteed majority (after verification), but it may fail to find one even if it exists.










NoteProblem E5



Let A[1..n] be an array of n distinct numbers. Consider randomized quickselect: pick a uniformly random pivot, partition, and recurse on the side containing the k-th smallest element.

What is the probability that a random pivot gives a “good split” (splits the array into two parts each of size at most 3n/4)?
Using this, bound the expected number of recursive calls.
How does the expected runtime compare to the worst-case runtime?









TipSolution






A good split occurs when the pivot is not in the smallest n/4 nor the largest n/4 elements. Probability = 1/2.
Each good split reduces the problem to at most 3n/4 size. Expected number of picks until a good split = 2 (geometric with p=1/2). So expected calls before size reduces: 2. Total expected depth: O(\log n).
Expected runtime O(n) (each level processes O(n) elements across all calls). Worst-case runtime O(n^2) (adversarial pivot choices).










NoteProblem E6



You flip a fair coin repeatedly. Let X be the number of flips until you see heads for the first time.

What is the distribution of X? Compute \Pr[X = k] for k \ge 1.
Compute \mathbb{E}[X] using linearity of expectation or the tail-sum formula.
Now let Y be the number of heads in n independent flips. What is \mathbb{E}[Y]? How does this illustrate linearity of expectation?









TipSolution






X \sim \text{Geometric}(1/2): \Pr[X = k] = (1/2)^{k-1} \cdot (1/2) = (1/2)^k.
\mathbb{E}[X] = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \Pr[X \ge k] = \sum_{k=1}^\infty (1/2)^{k-1} = 2. Or using tail sum: \mathbb{E}[X] = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \Pr[X > k] = \sum_{k=0}^\infty (1/2)^k = 2.
Y = \sum_{i=1}^n I_i where I_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(1/2). By linearity, \mathbb{E}[Y] = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}[I_i] = n \cdot 1/2 = n/2, even though the I_i are independent.










NoteProblem E7



Suppose we have a randomized algorithm that solves a decision problem with error probability 1/3 (i.e., it is correct with probability at least 2/3). How many independent runs are needed to boost the success probability to at least 1 - \delta? Use the union bound to give a simple bound, then use Chernoff/Hoeffding for a tighter bound.








TipSolution





Union bound: run k times and take majority. Error occurs if more than k/2 runs err. Each run errs with prob \le 1/3. By union bound, \Pr[\text{majority errs}] \le k \cdot (1/3)^{k/2} (bounding each pattern of \ge k/2 errors). Set this \le \delta and solve.
Hoeffding bound: Let X_i = 1 if run i errs, 0 otherwise. \mathbb{E}[\bar{X}] \le 1/3. By Hoeffding, \Pr[\bar{X} \ge 1/2] \le e^{-2k(1/2-1/3)^2} = e^{-2k/36} = e^{-k/18}. Set \le \delta \implies k \ge 18 \ln(1/\delta).









NoteProblem E8



You are given an unbiased coin. Design a randomized algorithm that uses this coin to simulate a biased coin that lands heads with probability exactly 1/3. What is the expected number of flips your algorithm uses per output?








TipSolution





Flip the coin twice. Map: HH \to H, HT \to T, TH \to T, TT \to repeat. \Pr[H] = 1/4 conditioned on not repeating, but we need exactly 1/3. Alternative: flip until you get HT or TH, then output H for HT and T for TH. Each of HT and TH has probability 1/4, so conditioned on stopping, each has probability 1/2. Not 1/3.
Correct method: flip until you see HHT or HTH or THH. Map HHT \to H, HTH \to H, THH \to T, and repeat on other outcomes. Each of the 3 patterns has probability 1/8 conditioned on one of them occurring, so \Pr[H] = 2/3 not 1/3.
Simpler: flip twice. If HH \to H, if HT or TH \to T, if TT \to repeat. \Pr[H] = 1/4 and \Pr[T] = 1/2, so conditioned on not repeating, \Pr[H] = (1/4)/(3/4) = 1/3. Expected flips per output: each trial uses 2 flips and succeeds with probability 3/4, so expected flips = 2 / (3/4) = 8/3.
